column4: The section's secondary dictionary entry for ك ذ ب says a decorated cloth can “lie by its state”; after the attempted seduction, this verse records the tearing of Joseph's shirt from behind, introducing the garment evidence developed in 12:26–28.
Moses tells Pharaoh إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ, the same exact trustworthy-messenger title the section finds repeated among the messengers in 26.
The section treats al-balad al-amīn as a secure city; this verse says God made the House a place people return to and a security, giving the sanctuary at Mecca the same protective function.
The section defines amānah against betrayal; in its debt instructions this verse says that when people trust one another, the entrusted person must discharge the trust and fear God.

The section's root gloss for ء م ن makes faith true assent and security a settled heart; this verse makes a precise exception for a coerced denial when the heart remains secure in faith, distinguishing an utterance from inward belief.

The section's dictionary example for ك ذ ب is cloth ornamented to look different from its true state; this verse says devils inspire one another with embellished speech as deception, a direct verbal counterpart to that deceptive surface.

This continuation says that hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter incline to the deceptive speech and become pleased with it; it shows a heart settling on falsehood rather than the section's secure truth.

The section ends by calling God the supreme judge and distinguishes genuine revelation from invention; this verse asks whether one should seek another judge when God has sent down the detailed Book in truth.
This verse says the Lord's word is complete in truth and justice and cannot be changed, the stable divine speech set against the section's human fabrications and denial.
The verse describes people who claim belief in revelation but seek judgment from false authorities after being told to reject them; this is a specific refusal to trust the revealed judge.
When called to Allah and the Messenger, the hypocrites turn away; this verse gives the same refusal of a trusted judgment that 4:60 introduces.

The section's dictionary gloss for د ي ن includes trusting someone in judgment; this verse assigns disputed judgment to God and immediately says “upon Him I rely,” joining true adjudication to trust in the Judge.
This verse says judgment belongs to God, who relates the truth and is the best of deciders; it brings the section's final claim about God's judgment into an explicit dispute over the warning.

The Prophet is told to follow the revelation, wait patiently until God judges, and trust that He is the best judge; this directly connects the reliable message with the section's final appeal to God's judgment.

At the Resurrection, the book is set, prophets and witnesses are brought, and God judges between people with truth so none are wronged; it supplies a concrete scene for the section's dīn and divine-judge themes.
This verse says God will judge between people on the Day of Resurrection over their disagreements, an explicit instance of the judgment the section associates with dīn.
The section says lying occurs in speech and deed; this command to speak a straight, sound word is followed by God's promise to set deeds right, a specific opposite link between words and actions.
The verse forbids mixing truth with falsehood or knowingly concealing truth; it states the boundary between genuine testimony and the fabricated or misleading speech developed in the section.
This repeats the command not to mix truth with falsehood or conceal it knowingly, showing the same specific boundary in an address to the People of the Book.

The verse commands people to fulfill God's covenant and not break confirmed oaths, noting that God is their guarantor; this is a concrete human counterpart to the section's note that al-Muʾmin is the One who fulfills His promise.
This verse commands fulfillment of a covenant and says the covenant will be asked about; it joins trustworthiness in a promise to later accountability.
The pledge to the Prophet is described as a pledge to God, whose hand is over theirs; whoever fulfills it receives a great reward, making loyalty to a trusted messenger an accountable act.

The verse describes believers who kept their covenant with God: some fulfilled their vow and some still await, without changing their commitment; it gives a specific human form of the section's trustworthiness.
The Shuayb who calls himself a trustworthy messenger in 26:178 commands his people here to give full measure; the passage joins the reliable messenger's word to honest dealing.
Shuayb continues by commanding just weighing; this supplies the second side of fair trade in the same speech begun at 26:181.
The same address forbids depriving people of their due and spreading corruption, completing Shuayb's specific contrast between honest conduct and betrayal.
Shuayb grounds the command in fearing the One who created them and earlier peoples; this connects the trade warning to its Creator and Judge.
In another address to Midian, Shuayb commands full measure and weight and forbids depriving people of their due; this repeats the trustworthy messenger's concrete demand for truthful dealing.
The verse commands full measure and weighing with a straight balance, directly countering the measure fraud that the section connects with denial of the Day.
This verse commands full measure and weight in justice, then forbids reducing people's due; its continuation also commands just speech, binding honest measurement to honest words.
The verse says God raised the heaven and set the balance; it locates the standard behind the fair weights that the section contrasts with cheating.
The next verse forbids transgressing the balance, marking the boundary against the cheating in measure named by the section.
The continuation commands establishing weight with justice and not making the balance deficient, completing the fair-measure scene.
On the Day of Resurrection, God sets just balances so no soul is wronged, even by a mustard seed's weight; this concretely answers the dishonest measuring associated with denial in 83.
People whose scales are heavy are placed in a pleasing life; this makes the scale of deeds a concrete image of the judgment that measure-fraud deniers reject.
The next verse names the heavy-scale outcome as a pleasing life, giving the reward side of the judgment introduced in 101:6.
The opposite case is one whose scales are light, a direct reversal of the fair accounting that dishonest traders deny.
The verse names the light-scale person's destination as the Abyss, completing the negative outcome of 101:8.
The next verse asks what the Abyss is, extending the judgment scene rather than leaving the consequence unnamed.
The final verse answers that the Abyss is a blazing fire, completing the fate attached to the light scales.
The verse asks whether the One who creates is like what does not create; it states the actual-making distinction that the section raises between God's creation and human fabrication.
Ibrahim asks his people whether they worship what they carve with their own hands; this is a specific confrontation between made objects and the real Creator.
The next verse says God created them and what they make, completing Ibrahim's contrast between their manufactured idols and divine creation.
This verse says God made the earth a resting place, formed people, and made their forms beautiful; the phrasing directly parallels the section's human made in excellent form.
God created the heavens and earth in truth, formed people, and made their forms beautiful; the verse then says they return to Him, joining the section's creation and judgment sequence.

The verse traces human life from dust through birth and maturity to old age, with some dying earlier; it gives a specific bodily decline that echoes 95:5's return to a low state, though it does not define that state identically.
The deniers ask whether they will really be created anew after being lost in the earth and then deny meeting their Lord; this is a direct objection to renewed creation and accountability.
God originates creation and repeats it, and the verse says this is easy for Him; it is another explicit formulation of the actual creation and return that answer denial in the section.
On the Day when wealth and children will not help, only the one who comes to God with a sound heart will benefit; this gives the section's settled heart a specific role at judgment.
Ibrahim is described as coming to his Lord with a sound heart; this is a second Quranic formulation of the sound heart that 26:89 makes decisive at judgment.
The verse says God's allies will have no fear and will not grieve; this is a direct assurance of fear removed, the section's stated root sense of security.
The next verse identifies those allies as people who believe and are mindful of God, specifying the faith behind the assurance in 10:62.
Their good news is promised in this life and the Hereafter, and God's words cannot change; this makes the security of 10:62 rest on a reliable promise.

A believer from Pharaoh's household argues that if Moses is lying, the lie is on him, but if he is truthful Pharaoh will face part of his warning; this is a concrete test of how to assess the trustworthy messenger's word.
Moses follows his trustworthy-messenger claim in 44:18 by telling Pharaoh not to exalt himself against God and saying he has clear authority; this states the warning carried by that reliable speaker.

The section's dictionary gloss for د ي ن connects the root with trust in judgment; in this Yusuf episode, دِينِ الْمَلِكِ means the king's legal order, a distinct but concrete legal sense of the same root.

This command requires believers to stand firmly for justice as witnesses even against themselves or relatives; it is a specific scene of truthful testimony under judgment that fits the section's trust-and-verdict link.

The section develops both deceptive speech and a garment that misstates reality; this verse begins the Adam scene in which Satan's whisper aims to expose what had been covered, setting up the false oath and leaf-covering in 7:21–22.
Satan swears that he is a sincere adviser, a direct false claim to trustworthiness; the next verse shows the deception's result.
The verse says Satan deluded them, their nakedness became apparent, and they began covering themselves with leaves; it joins a false assurance to clothing that cannot conceal the truth.
After the deception, Adam and his wife admit they wronged themselves and ask for mercy; their truthful confession reverses Satan's false assurance in the preceding verses.
Satan offers Adam the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay; this is a specific promise that misleads, opposite to the section's description of the One who makes His promise true.

After eating, Adam and his wife become aware of their nakedness and cover themselves with leaves; the bodily result completes the false promise in 20:120 and echoes the section's deceptive-cloth discussion.
The disciples ask Jesus for a table from heaven so their hearts may be reassured; the verse gives a concrete case where faith and a request for inward certainty meet.
